User: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Seattle WA. W-2 from Acme Corp: $88,100. Side income: $14,600 from web design (2 clients). Interest $1,780 (Chase savings), dividends $440 (Robinhood). Home office: 155 sq ft, rent $1,600/month, apartment 680 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,400 (EdFinancial, 2017–2020); charity $1,100 to Local United Way with receipt; unreimbursed expenses $720. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
Assistant: Thanks — this is enough to work with. Below I’ll:

- summarize which deductions you can/should claim,
- compare standard vs. itemized for your situation,
- explain home-office treatment (two methods) and show quick calculations for each,
- list the IRS forms you’ll need and where each item is reported,
- give a few practical next steps and recordkeeping notes.

Key facts you gave (used for calculations)
- Filing status: Married filing jointly (Seattle, WA — no state income tax).
- W-2 (Acme): $88,100
- Side income (web design, 2 clients): $14,600
- Interest (Chase savings): $1,780
- Dividends (Robinhood): $440
- Home: rented apartment, total 680 sq ft; home office 155 sq ft
- Rent: $1,600 / month → $19,200 / year
- Student loan interest paid in 2024: $4,400 (see note below)
- Charitable cash contributions (with receipt): $1,100
- “Unreimbursed expenses” $720 (I’ll clarify treatment below)

Which deductions apply and immediate conclusions
- Standard deduction (2024, married filing jointly): $29,200 (I used the 2024 amount).
- Your likely itemized deductions from the data you gave are small (charity $1,100 only), so the standard deduction is larger. Conclusion: take the standard deduction unless you have other itemizable items (mortgage interest, large property taxes, state income tax, large medical expenses, etc.).
- Student loan interest: the maximum federal deduction is capped at $2,500 per year (an adjustment to income / above-the-line). Because your MAGI (see calculations below) is well under the phaseout threshold, you can claim the maximum $2,500 even if you actually paid $4,400 in 2024.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses: NOT deductible on your federal return (through tax year 2025) if they are employee/unreimbursed expenses for your W-2 job. If instead the $720 are business expenses related to the web-design side gig, they are deductible on Schedule C.
- Home-office deduction: allowed only for self-employed (Schedule C) or certain qualifying situations. It’s not allowed for an employee working at home for a W-2 employer (except in rare cases). You have two methods: simplified or regular. See calculations next.

Home-office calculations — two methods
Home office size percentage = 155 / 680 = 22.794% (≈22.8%).
Annual rent = $1,600 × 12 = $19,200.

A) Regular method (allocate actual, e.g., percentage of rent and other shared home expenses)
- Rent portion for office = 19,200 × 22.794% ≈ $4,377.18
- If you have utilities, renter’s insurance, etc., those portions would also be pro‑rated and add to this amount.
- You must file Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) with Schedule C when using the regular method.

B) Simplified method
- $5.00 × square feet used for business (max 300 sq ft).
- 155 sq ft × $5 = $775
- No Form 8829 needed; report simplified amount directly on Schedule C.

Which method looks better here?
- Regular method (rent share ≈ $4,377) is much larger than simplified ($775). So, if you qualify (self-employed web-design work and the space meets the exclusive/regular use tests), the regular method will give you a bigger reduction to your self-employment income.

Quick impact on AGI — two practical scenarios
I’ll show two scenarios so you can see the effect on AGI and taxable income. I treat the $720 as business expenses for these examples; if it’s employee unreimbursed, ignore that $720 in the SE calculations and I’ll note the difference.

Base total gross income:
- W-2: 88,100
- Self-employment receipts: 14,600
- Interest: 1,780
- Dividends: 440
Total = $104,920

Important adjustments to income: student loan interest (adjustment, limited to $2,500) and half of the self-employment tax (computed from net SE profit).

Scenario 1 — Regular home-office method (and $720 as business expense)
- Business expenses = home-office rent portion $4,377.18 + $720 = $5,097.18
- Net self-employment profit = 14,600 − 5,097.18 = 9,502.82
- Net earnings subject to SE tax = 9,502.82 × 92.35% ≈ 8,778.19
- Self-employment tax (15.3%) ≈ $1,342.38
- Half of SE tax (deductible) ≈ $671.19
- Student loan interest deduction (max allowed) = $2,500 (since MAGI is below phaseout)
- AGI ≈ 104,920 − 671.19 − 2,500 = $101,748.81
- Standard deduction 29,200 → taxable income ≈ $72,548.81

Scenario 2 — Simplified home-office method ($775) + $720 business expenses
- Business expenses = 775 + 720 = $1,495
- Net SE profit = 14,600 − 1,495 = $13,105
- Net earnings subject to SE tax = 13,105 × 92.35% ≈ 12,101.60
- SE tax ≈ $1,851.35
- Half SE tax (deductible) ≈ $925.68
- AGI ≈ 104,920 − 925.68 − 2,500 = $101,494.32
- Taxable income after standard deduction ≈ $72,294.32

So: the regular method lowers your taxable income relative to the simplified method by a few hundred dollars in these calculations (because it yields a larger business expense and therefore a smaller SE tax deduction difference as well).

If the $720 are unreimbursed employee expenses (not self-employment) — then you should NOT include them on Schedule C and the regular home-office deduction would still be available only if the office is used for the self-employment activity. If the $720 are employee expenses for your W-2 job, they’re not deductible on the federal return (subject to the current law).

Other notes
- Student loan interest: The $4,400 you paid in 2024 reduces to a maximum deductible amount of $2,500 on your return. Keep Form 1098-E from EdFinancial (they should have sent you one) and your payment records.
- Interest > $1,500: because your interest (1,780) exceeds $1,500, you should file Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends) with Form 1040.
- Dividends reporting: include on Form 1040; if any dividends are qualified, they may get preferential tax rates (handled on Form 1040).
- 1099s: if you received 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC from clients, include those amounts on Schedule C. If you didn’t receive them but had the income, still report the income.
- Estimated taxes: with self-employment income you may owe quarterly estimated tax payments (to cover income tax and SE tax). If you haven’t paid quarterly, you may owe when you file and could owe underpayment penalties depending on amounts and withholding.

Which forms to use (summary)
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040) — to report adjustments to income (student loan interest deduction, and the deduction for one-half of self-employment tax comes through Schedule SE/Schedule 1).
- Schedule C — Profit or Loss from Business (report your web-design receipts and business expenses here).
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home (use only if using the regular method; attach to Schedule C).
- Schedule SE — Self-Employment Tax (compute SE tax and the employer‑equivalent deduction).
- Schedule B — Interest and Ordinary Dividends (required since interest > $1,500).
- Form 1099‑NEC or Form 1099‑MISC: you don’t file these but attach accurate reporting on Schedule C; keep any 1099s you received.
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (doesn’t look beneficial given your $1,100 charitable contribution vs. $29,200 standard deduction).
- Keep Forms 1098‑E (student loan interest), 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, 1099‑NEC, receipts for charitable gifts, and records for the home office (floorplan, square footage calculation, rent bills, utility bills, photos, and exclusive-use documentation).

Practical recommendations / next steps
1. Confirm whether the $720 is business-related (web design) or unreimbursed employee expenses for your W-2 job. If it’s business-related, include it on Schedule C; otherwise it’s not deductible.
2. If the home office is used exclusively and regularly for your web-design business, use the regular method (Form 8829) — it looks substantially more beneficial for you.
3. Collect paperwork: 1099s, W-2, 1099-INT, 1099-DIV, 1098-E, rent receipts, copies of charity receipts, records of business expenses, and documentation of the home office area.
4. Consider estimated tax payments for next year if self-employment is ongoing.
5. If you want, I can:
   - run a full estimated federal tax calculation (approximate tax due/refund) using the 2024 tax brackets and your preferred home-office method; or
   - prepare a checklist of exactly what to enter where on each form; or
   - draft a short summary you can forward to your tax preparer.

Disclaimer
This is general information based on the facts you provided; it’s not a substitute for personalized tax advice from a CPA or tax professional. If you want, I can run the more detailed tax liability estimate now (federal only) — tell me whether the $720 is business-related and whether you want the regular or simplified home-office method used. Which would you like next?
